My nephew lives across the country from me but we both share a love of video games. I bought Minecraft so we could play together and bond through what seems like a very great game. He's a bit of an expert and I'm a total noob. Any tips for a first timer so I don't make the game unfun for him while I learn?
Just bought Minecraft to play with my 8 year old nephew

There's a bunch of basic tutorials on minecraft's website, however I'm sure there would be more in depth ones on youtube. To be honest the only way you're really going to learn the game is just by playing it, maybe play some single player first and just get good at surviving the nights? After that your imagination will take you further.

1. Have the wiki open in another tab. Just do it; it will help greatly for crafting recipes.

  2. Assuming that you're in survival, one of the first things that you should do is get supplies for a stable food source. You can do this before building a shelter, often on the way to where you wish to survive. Grass (not dirt blocks with grass on the top, I mean the plant block that you can walk through) can yield seeds for wheat. Mobs can drop meat to survive off of until you have a stable farm. Crops should be grown near water blocks.

Edit: this may be a little confusing and out of order from what some suggest, but I listed this as one of the first things to do because of two reasons. First, because after you set some crops in the ground, you're free to kill time nearby, allowing you to take care of your business at night with other things at best or at worse focusing on evading mobs, to verify that your future shelter will be able to support survival (Press F3 for the Debug screen, which lists a bunch of info including your current biome. Preferably for beginners, choose a plains/savannah for easy navigation or an extreme hills biome for easy expansion if you make your shelter a cave), and second so that crops can grow as you're building your shelter, rather than building a shelter then making crops, for time efficiency.

  1. Depending on what difficulty you're playing on, control your rations accordingly. If you're playing on a difficulty where hunger will kill you (Hard or higher), focus on keeping that gauge up an try to be careful with how quickly you deplete it (jumping and sprinting both cause it to deplete at a higher rate). On normal and easy, you can get away with only filling it when you plan on leaving your base (assuming you've secured it) in order to heal, but in the meantime you won't be able to sprint.

  2. Speaking of which, make sure you have a key set to enable sprinting on holding. Double-tapping a button to dash/sprint is something that should have died in the 90s.

  3. Immediately, or else as you're getting your food source planned, get at least 6 log blocks. Craft 5 of them into wood planks (20 total). Craft 4 of them into sticks. Assuming I didn't mess up with math, you should have then 1 log, 16 planks, and 8 sticks. Use 4 of your planks to craft a Crafting Bench. Place the bench somewhere and use 4 sticks and 5 planks to make a wooden hoe and pickaxe. The hoe will be used for farming, as you should hopefully have seeds. If you're not near any hills or mountains, use your hands to dig into the dirt (stairway fashion, never dig straight down!) until you reach stone. Use your pickaxe to get at least 8 cobblestone, then go back to your bench. Make a furnace. Assuming that you're not near any open coal deposits or you haven't found one, create a piece of Charcoal from your wood log by placing the log in the top slot, burning one of your planks for fuel in the furnace. Use your sticks and the coal/charcoal to make 4 torches and use them to light up your shelter to prevent hostile mobs from spawning inside of it.

1. Combat - Combat in Minecraft is very basic. It's stupid. It's casual. You click on stuff and it does damage. Depending on what tool you're holding (swords typically provide the best bonuses for damage), whether you're sprinting, what armor/enchantments/potion effects you and the target have, and if the target is blocking (PVP only), you'll get a bonus for damage. PVP boils down to "can I output my damage faster than my opponent by getting as many perks as I can and by clicking faster than him/her?." Fighting mobs, however, often is more tricky. Skeletons and ranged enemies should be taken out with either ranged weapons or through the cunning speed of the player being able to weave around their projectiles and close the gap. Zombies are weak and don't do much, but they will attempt to swarm the player, so abusing weapon knockback and other means of crowd control is a plus. Spiders are filthy little shits, and deserve nothing less than the total apathy of the player and a bucket of lava to be dumped over their current position, but otherwise just pin them against a wall and click like mad. Creepers should be fought away from your constructions, but if you must fight them nearby try to do it near cobblestone structures to reduce the amount of structural damage their explosions do. Otherwise, knockback abuse is a fantastic way of dealing with creepers (sprint towards them, strike as soon as you are able, then step back. Worst-case-scenario is that the creeper cancels its detonation, and you must repeat, eventually getting you sweet sweet gunpowder, or you knock it into a wall or near some valuables and get something unsavory caught in the explosion. Best case scenario- you've effectively lobbed a grenade at a group of zombies). Baby zombies are little shits that the game could do without, so just look down and click like a madman. Endermen (the huge black teleporting mobs) can mostly be left alone if you just look at their lower legs. Looking at their torso/head will signal an attack. The game will make a horrible eerie noise to let you know you messed up, so run into the nearest lake you can find. Fighting them in the wilderness is dangerous because they will attempt to attack you from behind, and finding a secure defensive position leaves you vulnerable to other mobs. Fighting them in your own fortress is as easy as how wide your water bodies are in the fort; Endermen get damaged from water, so jumping in a lake will keep them away. For mobs in the Nether, I'll get to them later.

  2. If you're playing on PC, look at the "achievements." They serve no purpose besides helping indicate the next step in gameplay.

  3. Regarding shelter building - Your shelter should be one that mobs cannot get into, but you are able to. Something like a simple dirt hut with a door can work, but if you want windows you'd best be getting to learning landscaping. A pillar from the ocean floor may work, but mind you that even if there's a good sea between you and mobs and they are loaded, they will attempt to cross the ocean and siege your outpost, and supplies are difficult to get unless you've had experience with underwater construction. With experience and creativity, you'll be able to make more daring structures such as tree-houses and towers/castles, but what I've outlined in the next section incorporates plenty of defense tactics into one simple easy-to-make structure.

  4. Mob defense - For in-land bases, mind you that only spiders can climb 2-block high walls, and zombie "babies" can climb through 1x1 holes. Zombies will attempt to break down doors. Use the lack of decent AI to your advantage by walling your base and putting a roof on it (or an external ring to keep spiders from climbing over your walls, but a roof would be better for now since you'd need to fight mobs that spawn on your walls otherwise), then digging a moat around it at least one block deep. Do not fill the moat with anything except lava, for at long as you employ a combination of 2-block high walls and/or a door that cannot be entered without jumping through/into it, you'll be safe from most mobs. If you are using a door, make sure that you place it so that it doesn't leave a gap in the smoothness the wall in that there isn't a "step" that leads into it... you'll know what I mean when you place one. If not, then make sure the moat is at least 3 blocks deep for where you plan on entering, leave the gap open, and make the entrance wide enough that you can jump into it. Your worry then is making sure that skeletons don't shoot inside of it. The reason why this paragraph is so long is because I want to make sure that you know how to set up your base for preparing windows or other holes to determine the time of day, since locking yourself in a cave doesn't do you any favors for determining when you should go outside. Ideally, the structure should be about 4 blocks high from ground level, with some holes for windows at levels 2 (for better views of mobs, you wouldn't want to step outside while a Creeper is wondering right outside your doorstep, would you?) and/or 3 (protection against skeleton arrows, at least until you are able to make glass) and a roof at level 4.

1. Exploration - Know your tool materials. Wooden tools should be used up ASAP so that they don't clutter your inventory. Stone tools are often reliable and cheap to produce. Gold tools break blocks at an astounding speed, but gold is rare, and the tools are inefficient. Iron tools are very efficient and can break a huge assortment of blocks, but are difficult to obtain early-game and the material is often finite (so you may wish to save it for other items).Diamond tools are the best, but the material is harder to find than iron, and is generally a late-game material. Appropriate your tools you plan to take with you beforehand accordingly with what you plan to get; most above-world expeditions can be done with stone tools unless you're playing on a server where PVP is a prominent threat. Certain blocks can only be mined with a certain level of tool or higher (diamond can only be mined with iron or higher, for example). Underground expeditions can be done with iron tools, but keep your diamond tools secure until you've isolated valuable ore in case you end up swimming in a pool of lava. Caverns should be explored section by section, and lighting them, albeit time-consuming, is never a bad idea. Villages can be plundered, and the NPCs can be slaughtered (though not recommended if an Iron Golem is nearby), but the villagers can trade with you valuable resources. Their prices are steep, but finding one dressed in white (Librarian) that's willing to buy paper can set you up with a steady stream of supplies from the rest of the village, and they can be farmed like most other mobs in the game. Their crops also include the rare carrot. Underground Mineshafts are a different beast, and must be handled carefully. A special type of spider known as "Cave Spider" will spawn within certain spots within them. Cave Spiders are smaller than average spiders (allowing them to fit through tiny gaps) and can poison the player. Shafts will also include a spawner or three of the little demons. I suppose I should talk about spawners, though. Occasionally, you'll find dungeons, which are rooms that have a hostile mob spawner (indicated by a block that appears to have a mini model of the mob inside of a "cage") in a room with treasure inside. The spawners can be destroyed, or else used to form the basis of a mob grinder, allowing for easy obtainment of mob drops. Temples can be found in jungle, deep ocean, and desert biomes, and have their own style depending on the biome. Jungle ones will feature arrow traps, maybe some dynamite, and other dangers to hide treasures. Desert ones will feature empty rooms, save for a "basement" that can be accessed from destroying the ground in the central room. At the base of this "basement" will be treasure chests with goodies and a pressure plate that will blow the room up if stepped on. *Protip: Open up the room "ceiling" so that you can see the entire shaft. Place a single water block at the edge of one of the walls, so that you can slowly enter and exit the shaft from the flowing water. Navigate around the pressure plate, and putting yourself against the wall that the current pushes you towards, then break the plate to "defuse" the trap. Destroy the floor and loot the TNT, then loot the chests within the room. Afterwards, climb up the shaft. Ocean temples are rare, and should generally be avoided until you're more experienced with the game.

  2. Planes of existence - Each minecraft world has 3 areas that can be explored, the overworld, the Nether, and The End. The End is a location that may only be accessed by special portals found in special structures called "Strongholds," but you need not concern yourself with these until you are able to enchant tools. The Overworld is where most of the game takes place. The Nether is Hell. Literally. It's also an excellent source of lava source blocks. It may be accessed by making a 4x5 frame of obsidian blocks (though the corners need not be complete, and how the blocks were created (be it lava casting, placement from inventory, natural placement, et cetera) doesn't matter. Leave the inside 2x3 frame empty and light a fire inside of it). The Nether is dangerous, there's fire, explosions, and lava everywhere. This makes it an excellent place to get lava source blocks for projects/fuel and Netherrack, a block that can be lit on fire on the top, which will host the flame without letting it burn out (a blessing and a curse). Six mobs exist within it. Rarely, a regular skeleton in Nether Strongholds (huge brick structures that can contain mob spawners that can be converted to mob grinders), though I may be wrong.. A specialized melee Wither Skeleton is the standard here, standing at 3 blocks high, black in color, and dealing insane amounts of damage. You can hide in 2 block high spaces to escape them. Slime mobs, a rare mob in the Overworld, have a fire variant that can harm the player even at their smallest form. Zombie Pigmen exist as neutral mobs, and will not attack the player unless one of them is attacked first. Don't do it. Just... don't. Blazes are mobs that fly, smoke, and shoot fireballs at the player, making them one of the most dangerous mobs in the Nether that should be dealt with by ranged means and in secure battlefields away from any Netherrack floors. Ghasts are tricky, and shoot fireballs that will explode on impact, leaving more destruction than a Creeper's blast thanks to the lingering fire and for Netherrack being more easily destroyed than plenty of Overworld materials. Ghasts fly around, make noise, and blow shit up. My type of mob. With careful timing and one well placed attack, their fireballs can be reflected back at them. If they are over a large chunk of Netherrack, it's possible to rush towards then and strike them with melee attacks to quickly end then, but this is difficult and risky. They (and their fireballs) can always be shot with arrows.

Worth noting is a comparison of the battlefields of blazes and ghasts. Blaze mobs are typically found in Netherbrick Strongholds (Netherbrick is a maroon brick block found in the nether, but unlike Netherrack it will not stay lit), where the narrow platforms force the player to carefully dodge its fireballs with precision. On the other hand, Ghasts will destroy large portions of the battlefield, creating fire and possibly causing the player to fall into the magma sea below the Nether, and their attacks must be met with fleet footing some blocks away from the spot where the Ghasts aim. Because structures are generated randomly, the two battlefields may switch depending on the landscape. If so, try to avoid the area until the Ghast leaves and you can dispatch the Blazes. Both mobs drop materials for alchemy, so by the time you are able to beat them, you should have a decent understanding of the game (or else one where you're able to know how to research information that you need beyond the scope of this comment).

The last thing I wish to discuss is alternate weaponry. Lava is devastating as a liquid to place, and can destroy burnable structures/forests/landscapes if the player isn't careful. The player can also burn as well. Placing it carefully, however, can allow for the player to dispatch of large groups of enemies with ease and through resource-efficient means. Related is fire summoned by flint and steel. However, fire will not slow down a mob unlike one in lava, and will often leave the mob to wonder about while ignited, giving it time to be put out or attack (and ignite) the player in the meantime. Water can be used to control the flow of mobs, and one well placed water bucket can be used to gain the terrain advantage over a mob, being by gently pushing a group of them off of a cliff, by forcing them away from you so that you can pick off the ranged mobs with your own ranged weaponry, then do as you wish with the others, and tricking mobs into attempting to climb waterfalls so that you're able to hide, to damage Endermen, and so on... Snowballs do not deal damage except to Blazes and the Ender Dragon, but can be used to knock an enemy back with one of the most resource-efficient means in the game. Striking a zombie standing at the edge of a 12 block high cliff, for example, is generally more efficient resource and time-wise with a snowball than it is with a sword. You can also knock back Ghast fireballs without having to deal with wasting valuable arrows. TNT can be used for traps, or be placed then quickly triggered with either ignition (fire) or a redstone signal (often a torch. Redstone is something else entirely that I don't even want to begin discussing due to its scope) to destroy large areas of landscapes/enemies.

Some of the best stuff you can get comes from the nether. Make sure you have armor enchanted with "Fire Protection" and store your valuable gear that you can't afford to lose at your home while exploring the nether. More nether tips:

ALWAYS keep a flint & steel with you at all times! Re-igniting your nether portal without one is excessively difficult and requires luck. Ghasts can and WILL blow your portal out.

If you intend on exploring farther than eyeshot from your portal, write down the coordinates of your portal (hit f3 to find them), and you can find your way back. (torches on the ground as a trail of breadcrumbs also works well.)

You may also consider taking enough Obsidian into the nether with you to build an escape portal if things go awry. This will, unfortunately, give you a rather long walk back home. Each block you traverse in the Nether is equivalent to 8 blocks in the overworld, but the directions are the same. If you headed East in the nether, and have to escape back you need to go West 8 times the distance traversed in the Nether.

You need to find a Nether Fortress (head east or west, look for a large dark brick structure) and acquire one or more Blaze Rods. AS SOON AS YOU DO, go back home and build a Brewing Stand. This becomes your best friend later. You can put a Hopper on the top of the stand to help automate the ingredient addition process.

When in a Nether Fortress, avoid the tall black skeletons; these are Wither Skeletons and one hit will cause a Wither effect on you (similar to poision, except IT WILL KILL YOU BY ITSELF). Try not to get too close to those.

When you get your brewing stand up and running, go back into the nether and search for Magma Cubes. They act like normal Slime Cubes, but are immune to fire (like everything in the nether) and deal fire damage. They rarely drop Magma Slime, which is the primary ingredient for Fire Resistance Potions. If you intend on exploring the nether for any length of time, these WILL save your life & equipment. (Nether Wart -> Magma Slime -> Redstone Dust [for enhanced duration]) Consider this a requirement for deep exploration of the nether. They may be called "Resistance" potions, but they make you fully immune to all fire damage for the duration of the potion's effect.

Ghasts (rarely) drop Ghast Tears, which are INVALUABLE as the primary ingredient in regeneration potions. (Nether Wart -> Ghast Tear -> Redstone Dust [for enhanced duration])

Don't screw with the zombie pigmen! They are passive and will not attack you unprovoked. If you DO end up accidentally provoking one, they will ALL attack you. Unless you're looking to play Dynasty Warriors in Hell, get out immediately. They do, however, drop decent amounts of gold. So it's not all bad news.

Always look before you leap! There are a lot of dead drops in the nether, and you can find yourself on the receiving end of a fatal drop, or fall straight into lava! Lava is preferable because you don't take fall damage in it, and you should have a fire resistance potion on you to turn the lava lake into something more akin to a bubble bath.
